strengths: The paper targets an important problem and proposes a lightweight, conceptually intuitive combination of sparse attention, adaptive logit scaling, and hybrid positional encoding.

The synthetic evaluation spans several retrieval, memory, and ordering tasks, multiple positional encodings, and relevant attention baselines, with striking extrapolation results on MQMTAR, Reverse, and Max Retrieval.
The appendices provide numerous task-level results and ablations. The bounded-logit softmax entropy analysis and two-level-logit entmax example also offer useful limited-scope intuition.
weaknesses: Several central theoretical claims are incorrect or unsupported. In the over-squashing proof, the attention-support indices are reversed: sparse incoming support does not bound how many future queries attend to a token, so the claimed reduction from O(n^L) to O(s^L) does not follow. Moreover, fewer paths alone provides no lower bound on gradient strength, while the proof ignores derivatives through attention logits.

The representational-collapse result does not address the paper's own definition: it compares outputs for two different-length inputs rather than pairwise token representations within one input. Its derivation only treats one simplified attention layer despite claiming L-layer transformers, omits normalization and FFNs, and the main-text statement that the gap exceeds 'any constant c>0' is untenable.

Other theoretical sections contain serious gaps. The NoPE proposition assumes unproved uniform geometric decay, incorrectly reasons that deleting paths in one dynamic layer permanently removes cumulative influence, and invokes strongly connected components in a causal graph. The RoPE 'propositions' rely on uncontrolled Taylor approximations, omit sine and cross-component effects, and treat a single frequency component as if it determined the thresholded sum. The ALiBi proof also uses inconsistent threshold parameterization.

The evaluation protocol substantially compromises the empirical evidence: checkpoints are selected using 8x-OOD performance, and only the single best run across three seeds and multiple unspecified learning rates is reported. There are no means, variances, validation/test separation details, or complete search budgets, making the large gains vulnerable to selection bias.

Evidence is confined almost entirely to small synthetic models. The 120M FineWeb experiment only fits curves to independently learned positional scales, obtains a weak overall R² of 0.17 versus 0.12 for a linear fit, and provides no language-modeling or long-context downstream results for ASEntmax. No latency, memory, or realized-sparsity measurements support the practical long-context motivation.

The empirical narrative is overstated: NAPE itself drives much of the improvement across attention mechanisms, ASEntmax loses to simpler methods on several tasks, and some tasks saturate for every NAPE variant. Essential implementation details remain ambiguous, including whether n is total sequence length or causal prefix length; the latter makes (log n)^γ singular at n=1 for the learned negative γ values. Code, learning-rate grids, exact training schedules, and aggregate seed results are absent.

The empirical study covers numerous synthetic capabilities—retrieval, copying, counting, ordering, and state tracking—and compares softmax, scalable softmax, fixed entmax, and adaptive variants under several positional encodings and unusually large extrapolation factors.

Some results are striking: ASEntmax+NAPE retains 76.7% exact match on MQMTAR at 65K tokens after training up to length 64, and substantially improves Reverse at 4×–8× length. These gaps are too large to dismiss as evaluation sampling noise alone.
The bounded-logit softmax-dispersion observation and the elementary thresholding examples provide useful intuition for why exactly sparse transformations may behave differently from softmax.
weaknesses: A central theoretical claim—over-squashing alleviation—is not established. Counting fewer nonzero paths does not imply larger gradients; sparsity can instead delete the relevant path entirely. The proof derives only an upper bound, assumes attention coefficients are independent of hidden values, and provides no gradient lower bound or comparison to softmax. Moreover, the support indexing in Eqs. 60–61 is reversed: for forward influence from token i to a later token k, the relevant condition is i∈S_k, not k∈S_i.

The representational-collapse result does not match the stated definition. The definition concerns representations of different tokens within one sequence, whereas the construction compares the last-token representations of two different-length sequences. The appendix proves the construction only after one attention layer, yet the proposition and conclusions claim preservation after L transformer layers. The main-text wording that the gap exceeds c “for any constant c>0” is also stronger than the appendix’s existence statement.

Several positional-encoding propositions contain serious gaps. Proposition 6 assumes an unproved uniform geometric contraction; deleting a path or direct edge at one layer does not make the corresponding entry of all later products permanently zero because later layers can route through intermediates. The RoPE analysis applies entmax’s threshold separately to frequency components even though thresholding acts on their summed logit, treats a local Taylor approximation as an exact cutoff theorem, and omits sign/positivity conditions needed for its square root. Thus the claimed theoretical foundation for NAPE is unreliable.

The non-dispersion result is much weaker than advertised. The bound H(p)≤log|supp(p)| holds for every distribution, and the paper assumes rather than proves that entmax support grows sublinearly for learned transformer logits. Its existential “can concentrate” result does not justify claims that entmax maintains focus regardless of context length.

The evaluation protocol is statistically unreliable: the paper reports the single best run across three seeds and multiple unspecified learning rates, with no means, standard deviations, or confidence intervals. Checkpoints are selected using performance at an 8× OOD length that is also reported as a test condition, creating model-selection leakage and potentially favoring methods with higher variance.

All demonstrated task improvements come from small synthetic models. The 120M-parameter FineWeb experiment reports neither language-modeling quality nor long-context performance; it merely fits curves to 1024 freely learned positional scales. The proposed curve has only R²=0.17 versus 0.12 for a linear fit, which is weak evidence for the claimed parameterization. Standard long-context language, retrieval, or downstream benchmarks are absent.

The contribution is confounded between ASEntmax and NAPE. NAPE alone makes all methods tie on several tasks, scalable softmax is best on Copy, and fixed entmax frequently underperforms softmax. More systematic factorized ablations are needed, including matched tuning of NAPE head allocation/slopes and β/γ scaling components.

Reproducibility and practical evidence are incomplete: the bound s for γ is unspecified, behavior of (log n)^γ at n=1 with negative γ is unclear, the learning-rate search and training budgets are not fully reported, and no code or trained models are identified. Despite efficiency motivation, the paper gives no throughput, memory, kernel, or realized-support measurements.

The 420M-parameter, 7B-token language-model experiment provides evidence beyond synthetic tasks. Under matched NAPE settings, ASEntmax improves long-context perplexity and substantially outperforms the principal baselines on the reported needle-retrieval tasks.

The basic non-dispersion observation is useful and largely convincing: bounded-logit softmax approaches maximal normalized entropy, whereas an entmax distribution with sublinear support has correspondingly bounded normalized entropy.

weaknesses: Several central theoretical claims are not established. The representational-preservation proof treats essentially one attention layer although the proposition concerns depth L, and its original sparsemax sequence has dense support, violating the proposition's bounded-support premise. In the over-squashing proof, influence from token i to query k requires i to belong to k's support, whereas the defined path sets use k belonging to i's support. More fundamentally, fewer paths and an upper gradient bound do not imply stronger long-range gradients or alleviated over-squashing.

Proposition 5 is generally false under its stated assumptions: persistent paths with layer weights whose sum is finite need not make cumulative attention converge to token 1, while deleting a path at one layer does not prevent later layers from reconnecting it. The RoPE propositions also compare individual frequency components against a threshold applied to the summed score, omit potentially dominant sine terms, and assert unsupported monotonic behavior in α.

The synthetic evaluation protocol introduces serious selection bias: checkpoints are chosen using performance at an 8× out-of-distribution length, and the paper reports the single best result across three seeds and multiple learning rates. No means, standard deviations, complete search space, or separate OOD validation protocol are provided.

The key controlled baseline—softmax with exactly the same adaptive, content-dependent scaling parameterization—is reported only for selected synthetic tasks and is absent from the language-model experiments. Since SSMax is less expressive than ASEntmax's scaler, the real-world results do not cleanly isolate sparsity from added scaling capacity.

The real-world evidence remains limited to one relatively undertrained 420M model, one run per method, two needle-in-a-haystack subsets rather than the full RULER suite, and downstream benchmarks where several scores are near random. There is also no throughput, memory, or realized-sparsity analysis.

Important implementation details are ambiguous or inconsistent: it is unclear whether n denotes total sequence length or the query prefix position; the scaled-tanh function and its bound s are undefined; negative powers are problematic at log(1)=0; softplus cannot exactly realize the claimed β=0 reduction; and reported γ values do not clearly match the stated activation. The promised code link is absent and the learning-rate grid is unspecified.

Some conclusions overstate the evidence: sublinear support is assumed rather than demonstrated for trained models, an existential counterexample is described as preventing collapse broadly, and the main-text claim of 96.4% MQMTAR accuracy at 256× conflicts with the table, where 99.0% is reported and 96.4% belongs to Reverse. These technical and evaluation issues prevent the otherwise promising empirical contribution from meeting the top-tier acceptance bar.

weaknesses: The central over-squashing result is not established. Equation 87 is only an upper bound; reducing its number of terms cannot imply stronger gradients. The causal path sets in Equations 89–90 also use the attention support in the wrong direction. Sparse attention can simply delete the required long-range path, yielding zero sensitivity, so the stated assumptions do not imply less over-squashing. Average layer-gradient norms do not repair this logical gap.

The representation-preservation proof does not prove the stated depth-L transformer result. It analyzes essentially one simplified attention-averaging operation while omitting normalization, FFNs, projections, and the subsequent layers. Its explicit d=1 construction is incompatible with ordinary LayerNorm, which removes scalar variation. Moreover, the result is merely existential and does not establish that trained α-entmax models generally avoid collapse.

Several additional theoretical propositions are unsound. In Proposition 5, a connection missing at one layer need not remain absent at later layers, and per-layer connectivity without a uniform positive-weight condition does not imply convergence. Propositions 7–8 use a Taylor approximation and omit sine terms to claim exact RoPE cutoffs, and incorrectly threshold individual frequency components even though entmax thresholds their summed logit. Thus a major advertised contribution contains substantive mathematical errors.

The non-dispersion result is much weaker than presented: the entropy conclusion follows immediately after assuming sublinear support, but the paper neither guarantees nor empirically establishes such support growth for trained ASEntmax models. Bounded-logit, fixed-temperature softmax conclusions are also extrapolated too broadly to learned transformers.

Synthetic checkpoints and hyperparameters are selected using performance at OOD lengths, including 8×, and only the best run over three seeds and multiple learning rates is reported. There are no means, variances, or held-out selection protocol, making the headline extrapolation results vulnerable to substantial selection bias.

The real-data evidence is narrower than the claims suggest: there is one model scale and apparently one run, only two needle-retrieval subsets rather than the full RULER suite or realistic long-document tasks, and no uncertainty estimates. Results depend strongly on the custom NAPE setup; with standard RoPE or RoPE+ABF, ASEntmax often underperforms SSMax or fixed entmax.

The long-context perplexity scoring protocol is insufficiently specified to show that longer context causes the gains. If different token positions are averaged at each length, the decreasing trend can reflect changing targets or dilution of document-prefix tokens rather than improved context utilization.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the promised code link is absent; the bound s in the scaled-tanh parameterization is undefined; synthetic learning-rate grids, training durations, initialization, and the exact interpretation of n are missing. The motivating fit is also weak (overall R² only 0.17), and no actual support-size, throughput, or memory measurements demonstrate the practical benefit of sparse attention.

The over-squashing proof reverses the attention-support relation when defining reachable paths: a future token k receives gradient from i when i belongs to S_k, not when k belongs to S_i. More fundamentally, fewer paths provide no lower bound on useful gradient magnitude and can instead delete the required dependency. The displayed upper bound therefore cannot establish alleviated over-squashing or stronger gradients.

Other theory is substantially overstated or incorrect. Representational preservation is an existential, specially constructed example whose derivation only explicitly handles one layer, not a general guarantee. The entropy result is largely the generic bound H(p)≤log|support| conditioned on sublinear support. In the positional appendix, a zero direct edge at one layer does not force the cumulative coefficient to remain zero, per-layer connectivity does not imply convergence to token 1, and the RoPE analysis thresholds individual frequency components even though the attention logit is their sum and the entmax threshold is global.

The synthetic evaluation is not statistically valid as a clean extrapolation test: checkpoints are selected using performance at an 8× OOD length, and the paper reports the single best run across three seeds and multiple unspecified learning rates. There are no means, variances, or held-out model-selection protocol, so the extreme-length numbers are optimistically selected rather than unbiased estimates.

The language-modeling evidence does not isolate sparsity from the more expressive scaling mechanism. ASEntmax uses query- and head-dependent β and γ, whereas the principal SSMax baseline is much simpler; the matched ASSMax baseline is omitted from the 420M experiments. Results are also based on apparently one run per method, with no uncertainty estimates.

The headline 1000× result depends strongly on the hybrid NAPE positional scheme and one synthetic task. With RoPE or NoPE, MQMTAR rapidly fails, while on 2Back, Local Count, Copy, Sort, and Flip-Flop ASEntmax frequently ties or underperforms simpler alternatives. Consequently, claims of consistent superiority and general long-context robustness are stronger than the evidence.

The proposed scaling law is weakly motivated and incompletely specified. Its fit explains only R²=0.17 overall in the authors' own analysis, yet is described as fitting well. The text alternates between β,γ as head-specific scalars and query-dependent vectors; the bound s, initialization, learning-rate search, total synthetic training schedule, and exact validation splits are missing. The advertised code link is also broken.

Novelty is limited because entmax attention and length-dependent logit scaling are both established ideas. The real-world evaluation is narrow—near-random short-task performance, only two RULER subtests, no robust long-context reasoning tasks—and no latency, memory, or realized-sparsity measurements substantiate the practical long-context benefits. Together with several numerical and naming inconsistencies, these issues place the work clearly below the acceptance threshold.

weaknesses: The synthetic evaluation protocol has serious selection bias. Checkpoints are selected using performance at the reported OOD lengths, and the paper reports the single best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates, without specifying a separate OOD validation set or reporting means and variances. This substantially weakens the headline 1000× extrapolation claim.

The theoretical conclusions are much stronger than the results proved. The O(log s) entropy bound is true for any distribution with support s and is conditional on entmax maintaining sublinear support; the paper does not show that learned attention will do so. Likewise, the representation result is an existence counterexample, not a general prevention guarantee, and its proof only explicitly analyzes the first layer despite the depth-L statement.

The over-squashing argument is not sound. Reducing the number of paths from O(n^L) to O(s^L) does not imply stronger gradients or less over-squashing: sparse attention may remove the relevant path, and the derived expression is an upper bound rather than the lower-bound sensitivity guarantee needed for the conclusion. The empirical average-gradient-norm plot does not repair this gap.

Several appendix propositions appear incorrect or unjustified. In the NoPE analysis, deleting paths in one layer does not permanently remove first-token influence from a product of attention matrices, and no uniform geometric-decay constant is established. In the RoPE analysis, threshold crossings of an individual frequency component do not determine whether the summed attention logit crosses the global entmax threshold; Taylor approximations and omitted sine terms are nevertheless presented as propositions.

Important implementation details are ambiguous: scaled tanh and its bound s are undefined, parameter initialization is missing, and it is unclear whether n denotes total sequence length or each causal query's prefix length—an important issue when γ is negative and log(1) is encountered. The manuscript also provides no usable code link.

The empirical support outside synthetic tasks remains limited: no replicated 420M runs or uncertainty estimates are reported, RULER evaluation uses only two needle-retrieval subsets, the long-context perplexity protocol is insufficiently specified, and there are no efficiency measurements despite reliance on sparse attention.

The contribution combines two established ingredients—α-entmax and length-dependent logit scaling—so careful ablation is especially important. The language-model study lacks ASSMax, learned-α, and content-independent/head-independent scaling controls, while the positional-scale fit motivating γ has a low overall R² of 0.17. Consequently, the gains cannot yet be cleanly attributed to the proposed design choices.
